introduction: Two sets of identical twins have been separated since infancy: two brothers named Antipholus and the servants named Dromio who attend them. When the Syracusian pair enter Ephesus, their unknown doubles' home, ordinary errands begin to look like deception, madness or sorcery. A waiting wife, an anxious goldsmith and a purse of money pull the strangers into a city's familiar routines. Beneath the escalating confusion runs their father's search for his lost family, with his life threatened by the city's hostile laws.

fullSynopsis.text: Egeon, a merchant of Syracuse, faces execution for entering hostile Ephesus unless he can raise a ransom before evening. He tells Duke Solinus how a shipwreck divided his family: his wife and one twin son disappeared with one of the twin servants bought to attend the boys, while Egeon retained the other son and servant. The Antipholus and Dromio whom he raised later set out to find their brothers, and Egeon's own search has brought him here. The sympathetic Duke grants him the day to find assistance, though Egeon sees little hope.

Unaware of Egeon's arrest, Antipholus of Syracuse has arrived with his Dromio to continue the family search. His identical brother, Antipholus of Ephesus, already lives in the city with another Dromio and a wife, Adriana. When the Ephesian servant summons the visitor to dinner, Antipholus demands the money entrusted to his own servant and beats the apparent liar. Adriana, distressed by her husband's absence, finds the Syracusian pair and insists that he come home. The bewildered strangers, fearing enchantment, accept her invitation, and Dromio guards the door against all callers.

The real husband arrives with guests and is barred from his own house. Persuaded not to break in and damage Adriana's reputation, he instead dines with a Courtesan and proposes to give her the chain commissioned from Angelo the goldsmith for Adriana. Inside, Luciana urges the supposed husband to treat her sister kindly, but Antipholus of Syracuse declares love for Luciana herself. His Dromio reports that the kitchen maid claims him as her man. Both resolve to flee the uncanny city. Before they can leave, Angelo delivers the chain to the wrong Antipholus, who accepts it despite never ordering it.

Pressed by his own creditor, Angelo demands payment from Antipholus of Ephesus. Their equally truthful claims about a chain received and not received produce an arrest. The Syracusian Dromio then brings the arrested man news of a ship, receiving instead an order to fetch bail money from Adriana. He collects the purse but gives it to his own, unarrested master. The Ephesian Dromio returns with the rope his master previously ordered for beating his household. Antipholus of Ephesus takes this as further betrayal, and his violence strengthens Adriana's belief that he is mad.

The Courtesan, mistaking the visiting Antipholus for her dinner guest, has demanded either her ring or the promised chain and been driven away as a supposed devil. Adriana employs the conjurer Pinch, who binds the Ephesian master and servant as possessed. Their Syracusian doubles then appear armed, convincing the others that the prisoners have escaped. Further accusations over the chain force the visitors to seek sanctuary in an abbey, whose Abbess refuses to release them. When the Duke arrives on his way to Egeon's execution, Adriana appeals to him; the actual Ephesian prisoners, now escaped, also demand justice.

Egeon mistakes the Ephesian son for the one he raised and suffers his failure to recognize him. The Abbess finally brings out the Syracusian twins, making both pairs visible together. She reveals herself as Emilia, Egeon's lost wife, and the family reconstructs its separation. The chain, money and dinner confusions become intelligible. Solinus grants Egeon his life without requiring payment, the Ephesian Antipholus returns the Courtesan's ring, and the Syracusian Antipholus hopes to renew his suit to Luciana. Emilia invites everyone to a feast of reunion. Left together, the Dromios put aside precedence and enter hand in hand.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Duke Solinus condemns Egeon under the laws excluding Syracusians from Ephesus unless a substantial ransom is paid. Egeon explains that a shipwreck separated him from his wife, one twin son and one of the twin servants bought for their children. The son and servant he raised later left to seek their doubles, and Egeon has searched widely for them. Moved by his story, Solinus gives him until evening to raise the money. Meanwhile, Antipholus of Syracuse and his Dromio enter the city, warned to conceal their origins. Antipholus sends his servant to lodge their money safely. Dromio of Ephesus then calls him home to Adriana's dinner; the visitor mistakes him for his servant, demands the missing money and strikes him when he denies receiving it.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Adriana worries that her husband is late because he prefers another woman, challenging Luciana's argument that wives should submit patiently to their husbands' freedom. Dromio of Ephesus reports his beating and the supposed husband's denial that he has a house or wife. Adriana sends him back under threat of more punishment. Antipholus of Syracuse discovers that his money is safe, then confronts his own Dromio over words the servant never spoke and beats him too. Their banter about time and baldness gives way to a new confusion when Adriana and Luciana arrive. Adriana reproaches Antipholus as her unfaithful husband, claiming their lives are inseparable. Unable to explain how strangers know their names, he and Dromio follow her home as if entering an enchanted world. Dromio is ordered to keep all visitors outside.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Antipholus of Ephesus reaches his house with his own Dromio, Angelo and Balthasar, only to find Dromio of Syracuse refusing admission from within. Adriana and her servant also reject the callers. Balthasar persuades the husband to protect his wife's reputation by avoiding a public forced entry. Antipholus chooses dinner with a Courtesan instead and tells Angelo to bring the chain there as a gift to his hostess. Meanwhile, Luciana lectures the Syracusian Antipholus on showing affection to Adriana even if he loves elsewhere; he answers by declaring love for Luciana. His Dromio describes the kitchen maid's claim upon him, confirming their fear of witchcraft. Antipholus orders a ship sought for immediate departure. Angelo then hands the chain to the Syracusian, who accepts the mysterious gift and offers unsuccessfully to pay at once.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: A merchant presses Angelo for repayment, so Angelo seeks payment for the chain from Antipholus of Ephesus. The Ephesian has sent his Dromio for a rope to punish his household and truthfully denies receiving the chain. Angelo has him arrested. When Dromio of Syracuse reports a ship ready, the prisoner instead sends him to Adriana for bail money. Adriana, already upset by Luciana's report of the supposed husband's advances, supplies the purse. Dromio gives it to his own master, who cannot understand the talk of arrest. They reject the Courtesan's demand for her ring or chain as further sorcery. The Ephesian Dromio returns with his rope and receives another beating. Adriana and Pinch take the Ephesian pair's anger and denials as proof of possession and have them bound. The armed Syracusian pair appear immediately afterward, frightening everyone into believing that the captives are loose again.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Accused over the chain and pursued as madmen, the Syracusian pair retreat into an abbey. The Abbess refuses Adriana entry and blames her jealous reproaches for her supposed husband's condition. Adriana appeals to Solinus as he escorts Egeon toward execution. A messenger reports that the Ephesian prisoners have escaped and attacked Pinch, and they arrive to seek justice for their treatment. Egeon recognizes an Antipholus and Dromio but cannot obtain recognition from them. The Abbess emerges with their doubles, revealing herself as Emilia and restoring Egeon's lost family. The two sons explain their origins, while the day's confused exchanges of money, chain and hospitality are untangled. Solinus spares Egeon without a ransom. The Courtesan receives her ring, and the Syracusian Antipholus anticipates further conversation with Luciana. Emilia invites all to a feast, and the two Dromios join hands as equals.
